maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1954-55 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OP FINANCE

speechtext: A message from His Excellency the Governor General transmitting estimates for the financial year ending March 31, 1955, was presented by Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) and read by Mr. Speaker to the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1954-55 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as in past years, I do not propose to make any lengthy statement concerning the estimates. I might, however, note that the only change in the form of the new year estimates from that of previous years is in the manner in which the amounts included for salaries and wages of continuing staffs are summarized in the "details of services" section of the blue book.
Whereas the staff detail for each vote was formerly broken down to show numbers of position and paylist totals for permanent and temporary employees, a different form of summary has been substituted which discloses the same information for full-time, part-time and seasonal classes of positions. This change, of course, follows logically from the coming into force, on January 1, 1954, of the new Public Service Superannuation Act, the effect of which has been to eliminate the main distinction formerly existing between permanents and temporaries, namely, the pension benefit. The new breakdown between fulltime, part-time and seasonal positions will give hon. members more information upon which they may make judgments concerning the size and character of the civil service organization.
As regards the figures themselves, the total budgetary expenditure for the new year of $4,492 million compares with a total of $4,434 million for the current year, an increase of approximately $58 million or 1 [DOT] 3 per cent.
This increase is the result of a number of changes, both increases and decreases. The total requested for national defence, defence
production and civil defence is $1,955 million which is approximately $126 million less than the amount of $2,081 million approved for the current year.
This decrease reflects a tapering off in the capital assistance program for defence industry which reached its peak in 1952-53, and the more stable character of the defence department's equipment procurement program.
For purposes other than defence total budgetary expenditure provided for in the new estimates is $2,537 million compared to $2,353 million for the current year. This increase of $184 million is accounted for principally by $43 million additional for public debt charges, $27 million more for civil salaries, $22 million more for tax rental payments to provinces, a $22 million higher contribution to the civil service superannuation account, and $17 million more for family allowance payments. Also included in this increase are an item of $15 million for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and another of $7 million for the Department of Transport for which no comparable items were shown in the current year's estimates, although disbursements are being made under statutory authority.
I move:
That the message from His Excellency, together with the estimates presented this day, be referred to the committee of supply.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NAMING OF NORTHERN HALF OF ARCTIC ARCHIPELAGO

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NAMING OF NORTHERN HALF OF ARCTIC ARCHIPELAGO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the house I should like to make a statement respecting our most northern islands.
I am pleased to announce that Her Majesty the Queen has been graciously pleased to allow that her name be given to the entire group of islands which lies north of Lancaster sound and Viscount Melville sound. Henceforth this northern half of the Canadian Arctic archipelago will therefore be known as the Queen Elizabeth islands.
It seems particularly fitting that our present sovereign should allow her name to be permanently associated with this part of Canada. It was during the reign of her illustrious namesake that British seamen made their first voyages of discovery into what is now the Canadian Arctic. In the 350 years which have passed since then, our Arctic has been widely explored and mapped. Now, in the reign of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, we have every confidence that we are on the threshold of a new age, if not of discovery, then of development of our Arctic lands and seas.
It was important for the sake of administrative convenience that these particular islands should have some collective name. They stretch in a great triangle whose base, along the Arctic ocean's polar pack, is almost as wide as our three prairie provinces; to see even the outer edges of the group would require a flight of 2,300 miles. And yet these islands are in many ways a unit with its own peculiar conditions and problems. The lands themselves are, of course, the most northerly in North America and the most northerly of the Queen's realms. On their 160,000 square miles dwell less than 200

of her people, but beneath their surface may lie some of the richest treasures which we possess.
Hon. members will recall that the islands of our Arctic archipelago bear the names of other members of the royal family. Prince Charles island, in Foxe basin, was discovered and named about five years ago. Victoria island, Prince of Wales island and King William island are farther north, just below Viscount Melville sound. Now, northernmost of all, are the Queen Elizabeth islands, our final frontier.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NAMING OF NORTHERN HALF OF ARCTIC ARCHIPELAGO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announcement by the minister in regard to the gracious acceptance by Her Majesty of the suggestion that these islands should bear her name comes at a particularly appropriate time. There is something symbolic in the fact that these islands, extending to the polar circle in the north, should receive the name of our young Queen at a time when she is enjoying the summer sunshine of Australia, on the other side of the world. It symbolizes in a dramatic way the world-embracing character of this commonwealth partnership of which she assumed leadership last year.
The minister has spoken of the fact that this carries our imagination back 350 years to the earlier days of exploration under another Elizabeth. All the land areas may have been discovered, but the horizons are wider than ever before, and owing to the miracles of science new opportunities open out in every part of the world. It is not beyond the realm of hope that these islands, which will carry the name of our monarch, may not only symbolize the extent of our territory and of the whole north, but at the same time play an important part in the structure of Canada itself.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext: should like to direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries. Will the minister have an inspection made of the fish life in the North Saskatchewan river to determine whether the pollution of the water in that river is killing or affecting the health of the fish in that river?

subtopic: NORTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER-INQUIRY AS TO EFFECT ON FISH LIFE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for having given me notice of this question. There is no question that under the British North America Act legislative jurisdiction over fisheries rests with the federal government. However, by agreement with the government of Canada in 1930 the three prairie provinces took over the responsibility ;

of administering their own natural resources, including fisheries. Since that date provincial officers enforce federal fisheries conservation laws. The federal government does not maintain any staff in those provinces for this purpose. Therefore the inspection of the alleged pollution of the North Saskatchewan river would primarily be the responsibility of the governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta.
There is no question whatsoever about the fact that the Fisheries Act which is enforced in those provinces by the provincial authorities contains sufficient authority. Perhaps if I just read subsection 2 of section 33 of the Fisheries Act, it will be seen how wide the powers are. Subsection 2 of section 33 reads as follows:
No person shall cause or knowingly permit to pass into, or put or knowingly permit to be put, lime, chemical substances or drugs, poisonous matter, dead or decaying fish, or remnants thereof, mill rubbish or sawdust or any other deleterious substance or thing, whether the same is of a like character to the substances named in this section or not, in any water frequented by fish, or that flows into such water, nor on ice over either such waters.
In the five provinces-British Columbia and the four Atlantic provinces-where we have direct administration of the fisheries, we have found this section to be quite sufficient to control pollution of the water and I have no doubt that if the provincial authorities get together and use this section they will find the same thing.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, February 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Cote for the second reading of Bill No. 168, to amend the Post Office Act.
Post Office Act

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been stated in the past few minutes that a number of reasons have been outlined by the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) as to why he supports the bill to increase the postal rates. Analysing the statements that have been made by him as found in Hansard, I find that the Postmaster General put forward two basic reasons for the introduction of the bill. One is his claim that he requires to make up the sum of $13,500,000 which he maintains will be required to cover general salary increases, the cost of the five-day week and increased remuneration to mail contractors. He says that in addition the department will suffer a loss of $7,500,000 owing to the removal of stamps on cheques.
I should like to deal first of all with the $7,500,000 loss brought about by reason of stamps no longer being required on cheques. That is not a reason which should have been put forward by the Postmaster General. If this loss is, as I maintain it is, strictly the result of a cute, political trick pulled by the Liberals just before the election, then that should be their responsibility. At the time the government took that action prior to the election they were looking for kudos and backslapping because they were removing that charge and doing away with the inconvenience; but nothing whatsoever was said to indicate that the tax was going to be reimposed in another form after the election. Therefore there was, without a doubt, a general assumption on the part of the people that the loss would be made up out of the general revenue. I say it was a straight, cute political trick. It reacted entirely to the advantage of big business because the average citizen does not issue a great many cheques. It is companies, business, that issue the majority.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954

If he wishes to make a comparison or a passing reference to that as being the reason for the increase contemplated by the bill it is quite in order. I have let many others do that. speechtext: I do not want the hon. member to leave the impression that I permit members on one side to follow a certain trend of argument and do not permit members on the other side to follow the same trend. The hon. member knows perfectly well that he was dealing with the gesture made by the government last session as being favourable to big business. He went on to say that big business does not need to have that kind of gentle gesture made towards it. It was at that moment that I intervened. Now, I believe the hon. member and I understand the situation fairly well.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext:
In the arguments the Postmaster General used in support of the motion for second reading of this bill he mentioned the necessity for making up a loss of $7-5 million by an increase in the postal rate 'on first-class mail. I desired to state, Mr. Speaker, that in my estimation that loss is not one which rightfully should be given as a reason for an increase in the postal rate on first-class mail. Time after time the Postmaster General reiterated, not once but over a dozen times, his belief that those who used the mails should pay for them and that was the principle in this bill. If that is correct, then I would have expected that before this house was asked to impose a greater charge on first-class mail that principle, if it is not now in effect, would have been put into effect. That is not the situation, so the arguments that are used by the Postmaster General as to why this bill should be passed are the very reasons why we believe it should not be passed.
I refer the minister again to his own administration of this department, and to the statistics made available to this house and the public in the report of the Post Office Department. I am basing all I am going to say on the statements of the minister and the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) that those who use the mails should pay. According to the latest information I have on first-class mail at the present rate, for every 46

cents of revenue the cost of handling and distributing that mail is 29 cents. The revenue on first-class mail is 46 cents and the expense is 29 cents. We are informed that this works out at approximately $16 million of net profit on the handling of first-class mail. In such a situation where does the principle, that those who use the mails should pay, come into effect? We are being asked through the medium of this bill to authorize an increase that will bring in, according to the Postmaster General, a net revenue increase of $14 million. This net revenue increase of $14 million can only come from one source, and that is the increased postal rate on first-class mail. This is what the Postmaster General is asking, on the basis of the principle that those who use the mails shall pay. He is not satisfied with a net profit of $21 million; he wants a net profit of $35 million from those who use the first-class mail. 1 believe his own argument falls down completely.
In so far as second-class mails are concerned, the latest figures reveal that for 5 cents of revenue the cost of handling and delivering is 18-5 cents. The revenue is 5 cents and the expense is 18-5 cents, and this accounts for a deficit of approximately $16 million. The Postmaster General and the Secretary of State, in supporting this bill, say they believe in the principle that those who use the mails shall pay. I cannot see that argument, on the basis of the figures I have presented. If the Postmaster General really believes in the principle, then he should see that it is put into operation. If there is a deficit once the principle has been placed in operation, that is the time for him to come before the house with such a bill. I believe that to do so now, on the basis of this argument, is a most fantastic and ridiculous thing.
I was grateful that this debate could be adjourned last night because I desired to have the opportunity of reading the J. D. Woods and Gordon report which the Postmaster General tabled in the house yesterday and which appears as an appendix to Hansard. It is a most interesting report, although it is quite brief. Even before I read this report I was opposed to this bill, but after reading it I am more than ever opposed to it. It is quite obvious, at least to me, that something radical should be done in the post office administration branch. I cannot quite understand how this department has operated as efficiently as it has. The report, almost throughout, lays emphasis on the necessity for key personnel or the "top brass" of the organization. Just go through it very briefly, Mr. Speaker, and then try to understand

how the postal service has continued to operate. I am taking the word of the Postmaster General that J. D. Woods and Gordon is a good firm on business administration.
Let us look at the report as it appears on page 1806 of Hansard for February 4, 1954. It reads:
Operations Branch
(a)	Chief superintendent-engineering-a man should be obtained from outside the service to fill this vacancy . . .
(b)	Mechanical engineering division-This position should be filled either from outside the service or possibly by one of the engineers from one of the major post offices . . .
(c)	Methods and time study division-A start should be made immediately on the organization of this division. Either the man to head the division or one or two of his assistants should be drawn from outside the department . . .
(d)	Chief superintendent-operations-This position should be filled by the most experienced man available within the service . . .
(g)	Methods and procedures division-The organization of this division is dependent on obtaining suitable personnel to carry out the work . . .
(h)	Inquiries division-As soon as a suitable postal superintendent can be selected, this division can be formed.
Transportation branch
(a)	Chief superintendent-transportation planning and research-This position should be filled as soon as possible . . .
(b)	Chief superintendent-transportation services -This position should be filled by a man with proven administrative ability . . .
Financial branch
(a) There are three senior positions to be filled in this branch and the organization changes can take place as soon as suitable men are available. In addition there is the position of comptroller in the administration branch. It will probably be necessary to go outside the department to fill two or three or these four positions . . .
This is the way the report reads; key man after key man; reorganization after reorganization, and recommendations to go outside the department to obtain suitable men to do the job. Is it any wonder, Mr. Speaker, that we feel the Post Office Department must have done a remarkable job in the past in operating as efficiently as they have? In view of that brief report which the Postmaster General received in December 1952-I have not seen the main report-I say there is conclusive evidence that some reorganization should be undertaken by the government. I say, on the basis of this report, that they are not carrying out their own principle that those who use the mails shall pay. I believe, therefore, that this bill should most certainly be emphatically rejected by every member in this house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take part in the present debate but so much fuss has been made about the report which was 83276-115
Post Office Act
tabled the day before last that I believe it is mv duty, as a businessman, to rise and voice my protests.
(Text):
Before proceeding further I should like to say that for the last three days hon. members have been commenting upon the report as if it were the Bible. Let me say that I have now before me a report which, as a businessman, I have just had prepared by a firm of management engineers. It is a very complete report. I have not studied it yet, but I am sure when I do study it that I possibly will not implement more than 40 per cent of what it contains.
I understand that about two-thirds of the recommendations contained in the report submitted to the Post Office Department have been implemented. This shows that it was given very close study, that it has been implemented after the study was made, and that the decisions were made by superior officers in the department.
We have just been told that one of the recommendations in the report was that some of the senior officers were to be changed. Well, in these days, in business, every day we are confronted with such things. We have to make continual changes in the administration of different corporations in which we are interested. And not only that, but in the larger corporations a complete bookkeeping system may be installed today, and in eight months' time it may be found that that system is not as efficient as it was supposed to be. As a result it is thrown out, and another one comes in.
So it is not surprising to find, in a vast department such as the Post Office Department, one which covers the whole of Canada, one which employs thousands of persons in thousands of localities, and handles mail in all parts of Canada as well as mail from the United States and other parts of the world- I say it is not surprising, in a department of this kind, to find at certain times that the degree of efficiency is not all that it should be.
Hence this report was called for and made; and we are told that to the extent of two-thirds the Postmaster General has implemented the recommendations it contained. I say he is to be commended upon his efficiency. This is particularly true when we consider the billions of letters handled by the department, and place alongside that the very slight loss that has been suffered in the last few years.
And yet some hon. members are very critical. For instance, if a letter coming to one of them is delayed, then immediately he

Post Office Act
attacks the department, and says all kinds of things about it. But we do not hear anything about human frailties, with the thousands of employees in the department, the number of trains it uses, the number of post offices, and the great number of articles passing through them. We hear nothing from them about the great number of hands through which a letter passes before it reaches its destination. To my mind it is nothing short of wonderful that in Canada at this time we have such a satisfactory system, with so few complaints coming in-and hon. members are in a position to know, because we receive complaints from practically all parts of Canada.
I do not want to be too long in what I say today, but I do not think the working population in Canada is going to object too strenuously to the increased postage they will be called upon to pay. I do not think the average employee writes more than ten or twelve letters a month; and if he is called upon to pay only one cent more, then I do not think the ten or twelve cents a month more, the $1.20 a year, will annoy him too greatly because he will be conscious of the fact that he is anxious to have increases in his salary, and that he has enjoyed such increases in the last few years. He will bear in mind that post office employees are also entitled to increases, and that if those employees are to receive higher pay it must be taken from the public by way of a higher postal rate.
The cost of living has increased to people in every walk of life, and I am sure that all employees in Canada will be glad to contribute their bit to enable the Post Office Department to continue the efficient service it has been giving the people of Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. M. Hamilton (Notre Dame de Grace):
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, listening to the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) last night I thought of something I received through the mail not long ago. It was a civil service notice advising that a commercial artist was required in the Department of National Defence.
I wondered about it, and discussed the matter with a colleague of mine. He gave me an answer in these words, "Well, with the estimates coming down, the Department of National Defence needs a commercial artist to paint a brighter picture." It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we will not find such a gentleman attached to the Post Office Department, because the Postmaster General needs no commercial artist: he paints his own picture. And he paints pictures that sometimes are not quite in accord with the facts, as many people see them.
IMr. Bourque.]
This report has been tremendously valuable, I think, in establishing certain facts. One point which has not been brought out, and which might just be mentioned, is that apparently it cost over $70,000. In my original remarks I made reference to $10,000 or $15,000; but we find in the figures for the department a total of $72,000.54 paid to this company in the last two years. I want to get my money's worth out of it, as I believe most of us do; and that is why we are using the facts contained so plentifully in that report.
Before going further I wish to make one point crystal clear, so that subsequently it will not be distorted by the Postmaster General or by anybody else. He has tried to make it seem that it is inconsistent to compliment certain aspects of his departmental operations while condemning others. He said that several times and in various ways yesterday. I say there is no inconsistency in this. I, personally, am quite happy to stand here and praise the great bulk of post office employees who are doing their work under such trying conditions, and, although being so maladministered, are still doing their best to do a good job. I praise those employees for what they are doing.
I cannot help thinking of the words, as I remember them, written around the post office building in Washington. Perhaps I am not reciting them exactly, but I believe they run something like this: "Neither hail nor heat nor snow nor darkness of night shall slow these carriers from their appointed rounds."
Most of the people in the Post Office Department are doing a good job; but I criticize in the very strongest terms the Postmaster General for his administration of the department, and for many of the ways in which it is administered under his direction. I would remind him again, so that there may be no distortion, that these are two totally different fields

the staff who do the work, and the man who is responsible for directing the department.
And just thinking back to the quotation to which I referred a moment ago, it will be recalled that there was a reference to the darkness of night. I just cannot help feeling that if there is any darkness around this department, then it is that which has been caused by the minister himself, in an attempt to defend what is obviously an indefensible measure.
First of all I should like to deal in general terms with the arguments the minister introduced yesterday.

On page 10 of the report it says:
The terms of reference were, in short, to see what improvements if any could be made in the existing postal services.
The report lists 73 recommendations under various headings so therefore we have indication that great improvements are possible. Further on page 13 the report says:
Our principal object in this survey was to consider the over-all organizational structure, not to make detailed studies of ways and means of cutting costs.
And again:
We have, however, during the course of our survey noted a number of instances where we feel confident substantial savings and improvements in service can be introduced providing the organizational structure is strengthened.
It is obvious that this report was not even designed to point out ways and means of cutting costs. That means that if those things arose as purely incidental to the report, beyond this report there must be a tremendous field in which costs can be further reduced and in which more work can be done to assure efficient administration. It is obvious that there are hundreds of thousands of dollars to be saved, that there are millions of dollars to be saved that I do not think the minister has even told us about.
Let us continue with the minister's remarks. Having had about two weeks to study our argument, the minister came back with what seemed to me to be a very poor case. We have had only overnight in which to study it, but his case is such that it takes no great strength to refute it. I should like to deal with the argument the minister introduced yesterday, and first of all I shall quote from his remarks on page 1765 of Hansard, as follows:
Let me first state that in presenting this report the firm of business consultants estimated that in terms of salaries and additional staff required, increased amounts of approximately $300,000 per annum at headquarters and approximately $400,000 in the field would be required-
I fail to find that statement anywhere in the report. I challenge the hon. gentleman to show me where that statement is contained in the Woods and Gordon report. This means that we have here a perfect example of atrocious turnings and twistings which my leader so aptly termed yesterday as a tawdry political statement. But more important than that, it indicates something else. As far as I can see, it indicates that the Postmaster General somewhere has another more secret document from which he himself could draw those figures. I am quite sure, or I would rather hope, that he did not just draw them from his hat.

I should like to know whether this is a piece of isolated information which just came to him on a piece of paper or whether it comes from another secret document which in addition to this information contains other information which should be laid before this house and which specifically estimates possible savings as a result of the changes which the company that made the study suggests. I would like to know, in short, what the Postmaster General is hiding.
Then yesterday the Postmaster General attempted to deal with a statement I had made during the debate on the resolution. I think the easiest way to deal with this would be to read my remarks and then read his interpretation, which is completely different. I shall then tell why I said it. On January 15, as reported on page 1178 of Hansard, I said:
Before I resume my seat I have just one further question. I should like to ask the minister when we in Notre Dame de Grace are going to get our second mail delivery a day.
By the time the minister got here he referred to my remarks as follows, and I quote from page 1769 of Hansard of yesterday:
-he concluded by asking that the same postal department spend $4 or $5 million more to give the service of a second delivery a day in residential areas.
It will be seen that there is absolutely no relationship between those two statements. The reason I interjected that remark when I was speaking was that on December 4 I had written asking substantially the same question. Almost two weeks later I got a reply from the minister in which he said that the postmaster at Montreal had been asked to submit a report in that regard and when it was received I would be further advised.
It seemed to me that from December 15 to January 15 was long enough, even under present circumstances, to get a letter from Montreal to Ottawa and back, and so I asked the Postmaster General about it. The result is that my remarks were distorted and twisted to mean something which was never meant.
We have another interesting statement in the Postmaster General's remarks. He referred first to the financial statements which he publishes for the public, and then on page 1765 he is reported as follows:
We do, however, maintain for our own guidance office estimates of what these various services amount to.
And then in the same paragraph:
In recent years, however, these statements showed deficits not surpluses.

Post Office Act
Is that not interesting? Apparently the hon. gentleman keeps two sets of figures. As he says, there are two sets of statements, one for the public, which he publishes, and another which apparently shows a truer picture, according to the hon. gentleman, for his department, and which he does not publish. That is what he says here that he has two statements, one which is published and another which is not.
This rather reminds me of the person who was applying for a job as a bookkeeper. He was asked if he could do double entry bookkeeping, and he replied, "I do double entry bookkeeping and even triple entry bookkeeping." He was asked what that was and he said, "In my last job I kept one set of books for the boss showing the true profit; another set of books were kept for the shareholders, showing no profit; and there was another set of books for the government tax collector, showing a loss." It seems to me that the Postmaster General has got as far as double entry bookkeeping with his two sets of statements.
So far we have seen two things. We have seen that the Postmaster General has been attributing figures to the Woods-Gordon report which were not contained therein. We have seen that he has another set of statements which apparently show a different picture from those which he published. If the hon. gentleman has information which denies that which he has given this house, and which bears on the problem, let him produce it so that we can see it and make our decisions and so that the people of Canada can make their decision on the facts of the case and not on his twisted interpretation of them. I feel rather badly about that twisting of my statement yesterday, and I am sorry if I am showing it just a little bit. Those remarks yesterday were quite misleading. Referring again to the question of ways and means of obtaining money to meet the additional expenditures which the hon. gentleman listed, he said, as reported on page 1769 of Hansard:
There are two ways of obtaining the money to meet these additional and essential expenditures. One is by an increase in the postal rates; the other is by general taxation. So far I have not received from anyone in the house any other suggestion.
Let there be no doubt in the hon. gentleman's mind. If he did not read or could not understand or did not appreciate my previous remarks, I am now going to make an additional suggestion. I make the additional suggestion that he institute efficient administration in his department in order to accomplish these savings which, he says, he requires to meet his additional expenditures.

Of course, Mr. Speaker, the truth of the matter is that the hon. gentleman seems to have difficulty in even understanding what efficient administration is. Let us see why I make that statement. Yesterday the minister said, as reported at page 1766 of Hansard: The fact is, as the report repeatedly states, that the department is well administered and departmental officers have vigorously pursued a program of efficient operation over the years. What better evidence of this is required than the fact that during the past 20 years the volume of mail has increased by 178 per cent whereas the increase in total staff approximated 100 per cent?
Apparently that is the position on which the minister stands. He claims his department is well administered, and asks: "What better evidence can you require than this?" But, Mr. Speaker, the Post Office Department is engaged in the carriage of mails. The railways of this country are engaged in the carriage of passengers and freight. Let us see over the same 20-year period what the railways of this country have done. The steam railways of this country-my figures come from the Canada Year Book-have increased their combined passenger and freight mileage, passenger miles plus freight ton miles, by 211 per cent between 1931 and 1951, and during that time they have increased their staff by only 31 per cent. Here we have a comparison. We have the post office volume increased by 178 per cent and staff by 100 per cent, and we have the steam railways volume up by 211 per cent, and staff by 31 per cent. Both are engaged in fundamentally the same type of business, the carriage of commodities.
That demolishes, I believe, for all time the minister's claim, because similar instances could be introduced from many other fields showing that this vaunted record which the hon. gentleman is so proud of is inferior, owing to bad administration. He claims it is good administration which has produced this record, which, in fact, is inferior to most other industries and most other businesses.
Let me remind the minister that I am not criticizing the employees of the department. I am laying the blame on the administration of the department which is directly under the hon. gentleman who sits opposite me.
The hon. member on my left dealt at some length with the appendix which the Postmaster General tabled last night. I am not quite sure, because the minister did not indicate-and that may be rather curious-to which year that report referred. He said "December 17" on two occasions, but not once did he say which year it referred to. Surely he knows which year. However, let us look

at it. It the document he tabled, containing a set of recommendations on the implementation of the reports, was received at the end of 1952, then the estimates for the coming year, which I have in my hand and which I have had only half an hour to study, contain very few of the recommendations contained in this Woods and Gordon report. It is quite obvious that if the recommendations in that report were to be implemented by March 31, 1955, then these recommendations would show up in the estimates. The Woods and Gordon report make suggestions for changes in position, for changes in title, and for changes in administration generally. I have studied the Woods and Gordon report, I sometimes suspect, almost as well as the hon. gentleman who holds the position of Postmaster General, and I have searched for half an hour and I cannot find any indication in these estimates that the implementation of this report is going through at the present time.
If this document which he presented is dated 1953-that is quite possible-then he received the report and waited thirteen months before he even asked for a set of recommendations as to how to implement them. Let the hon. gentleman take his choice, but I do not think it reflects too great credit upon his administration.
Turning for a few minutes, Mr. Speaker, to a few points which are brought out in this report, I would like first of all to deal with the carriage of mail. It is quite apparent from the report that the department seems in the dark as to the amount of subsidies it is paying to various carriers. For example, we find this at page 50 of the report:
After a service has been in operation for a number of years the fact that it was the intention to pay a subsidy while the service was being introduced is lost sight of and future contracts are based on the existing contract. The subsidy may therefore be perpetuated long after the justification for it has ceased to exist.
Then on page 56, the report reads:
The present form of contract with the railroads results in a subsidy being paid which is not clearly recognized.
A few sentences after that we find this:
The department as a result is normally paying for space which will be required only on rare occasions.
I would draw particular attention to that statement, Mr. Speaker. What a horrible thing to have to say about that being done with the taxpayers' money. And then the hon. gentleman comes in and says, "I need more money from the taxpayers through the increase in postage rates in order to carry out such a practice."
The most obvious injustice, of course, Mr. Speaker, is in the case of air mail. In a
Post Office Act
previous speech in this house I pointed out that the department pays the Trans-Canada Air Lines some four times as much per ton mile as the average of other air freight which they carry. Let us examine this for a moment. The post office deals with Trans-Canada Air Lines, and Trans-Canada Air Lines is a hybrid organization. Its stock is held by Canadian National Railways which reports to the Department of Transport, sometimes-when it feels like it, I rather suspect. I have seen other occasions when it did not report when it was requested to do so. But at least in theory it reports to the Department of Transport. That is the C.N.R. On the other hand, the T.C.A., which the C.N.R. owns, reports to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and Defence Production.
Therefore, at a time when a question of rate adjustment comes up-and this is one time, frankly, when I feel just a little bit sorry for the Postmaster General-we have the hon. gentleman on one side who presumably would like to see his mail carried for the lowest amount of money, while opposed to him automatically, within this set of circumstances, we have two ministers whose interest is in carrying the mail via air mail at the greatest possible rate. We have the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to whom Trans-Canada Air Lines report and we have the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) who, through the Canadian National Railways, is going to be affected by the operating results of Trans-Canada Air Lines. The matter is extremely complicated. It took me quite a little while to figure it out. But it is also very plain that you have two ministers on one side and one minister on the other. Perhaps that is the reason-I do not know-why we see this absolutely astonishing situation in which our post office pays per ton-mile some four times as much as do other people who use the same equipment and the same type of services.
I would just remind the gentleman who is the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) that it is possible to be so amiable about things that one becomes absolutely ineffective in protecting the interests of one's own department and in looking after the interests of the public themselves.
Let us take another interesting case. On page 41 of the report, referring to relations between the Department of Public Works and the Post Office Department, we find this:
The two departments might well consider an arrangement whereby the supervision of caretaking, maintenance and service staffs would be the responsibility of the Post Office Department . . .
In the Financial Times for January 29 we find a story with regard to towels, soap, etc., which says, "The servicing job has been

Post Office Act
handed over to public works". In other words, after paying our money, $70,000 of it, for a report-and I would think, on balance, it is an excellent report-made by experts in administration, we find it recommending one thing. Then eighteen months later we find the department doing the exact opposite. The report recommends that the Post Office Department take this thing over. But the exact opposite is what happens. The Department of Public Works takes it over, which is just the thing that has not been recommended by the report. Actually, it is the thing which the report says one should get away from. How can the minister sit there and think of the things he said last night and not feel shamed by these things?
There is one other thing in the report to which I should like to refer. We find the report saying this:
Under the present procedure before tenders can be invited the purchasing and stationery division must forward a list setting out the names of the suppliers who are to be asked to tender to the deputy postmaster general; he in turn passes it to the Postmaster General for approval. This practice is presumably to allow the Postmaster General to add to the list of suppliers any names he may wish. This procedure adds to the delay in calling for tenders.
I am not going to expand on that paragraph unduly, Mr. Speaker, but I think it is unfortunate that the administration of the Post Office Department should be held up in order that the Postmaster General can add the names that he wishes-and they might very well be personal friends of the government- to the list of those who are going to tender for particular contracts.
The United States has been referred to periodically in the course of this debate, Mr. Speaker. I took a great deal of pleasure last night in voting in support of a motion which proposed that the bill which is now before us might receive further study in a committee. Without trying to go to too great length, I might list some of the things which have been done in the United States before they have come to their conclusion, and I might say that they are still debating. They held public hearings on the subject last summer. They had an independent organization prepare a report on public reaction and public feeling about this matter. They set up a 10-man advisory council of the post office committee, which reported. They obtained a Senate report on the subject. There were various other incidental things. Of course they retained a prominent firm of chartered accountants to study costs, allocation of expenses, existing subsidies and so on, in order to give them adequate information.

The important point which I should like to make is this. This report which they obtained went far beyond the confines of the Woods-Gordon report; and it was made freely available to all who wished to see it without any sputterings, camouflage, delays or insinuations. Here we are being asked to decide an increase of many millions of dollars in the postage rate. Since the Postmaster General has made so many obvious slight errors up until now, I just wonder whether it is not possible that, in his calculations, he might again have made an error of a few million dollars, which error would invalidate the stand that he is at present trying -I think so unhappily-to defend.
I might say also that in the United States their committee suggested only 28 changes, one-half of those suggested in the Woods-Gordon report and, according to Advertising Age of January 25, 1954, their committee reported that "hundreds of millions" of dollars could be clipped from post office operating costs.
Even allowing for variations as between the United States and Canada, surely there is some opportunity up here for doing the same. I will give the Postmaster General one example. If he would be realistic about the printing of his stamps, he could cut his costs in that department alone in half, and that would represent about $375,000 a year. I am quoting here from an article in the Wall Street Journal which refers to investigations being done on this matter in the United States. To take one paragraph referring to this rotogravure process, it says this:
And, says the man from the engraving bureau, rotogravure stamps cost less than half as much to turn out.
And later:
To the layman, the rotogravure stamp will look as good as the current stamp, indeed far prettier.
Mr. Speaker, I think I have perhaps stayed away from the arguments that have been used in the past. I think perhaps I have introduced a little bit of new material. I think perhaps last night I found one of the reasons for the problems in the Post Office Department when the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) said that he had occupied the position of Postmaster General for a few weeks. I just want to say that I look forward with particular interest to what may be said by the gentlemen who support this government, because we have heard very little from them so far.
Perhaps it all falls into the same category as the statement made to me once by someone outside this house who had not had the benefit of a great deal of education. I am

not suggesting that there is anybody in that class in the house. But he said to me: "You know, when you ain't got an education you just got to use your brains." We on this side of the house first of all have our education, but on this measure we are also using our brains, and our brains logically lead us to the conclusion that the present request of the government for an increase in the postage rates is completely indefensible and completely unsupported by any substantial documented or intelligent evidence. For that reason I, and I would imagine my colleagues as well, am certainly opposed to this increase.

charge. I want to say to the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) that I am not particularly critical, shall I say, of him personally. I do not think that is the point. Mr. Speaker, I think there is quite a bit of merit in the amendment that has just been moved, and in speaking on it I should like to deal in some detail with the remarks made by the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) in the statement which he presented to the house yesterday. He said in part, as found at page 1764 of Hansard for yesterday:
We think the readjustment of the postal tariff, increasing the postage rate, is the most equitable arrangement . . .
We have said on numerous occasions since this debate started that we do not agree with that statement at all. I might point out that the principle of equalization of rates has been

Post Office Act
accepted in many spheres of public service in Canada as well as in other countries. Surely that same principle can be fairly applied to the allocation of revenues and expenses among government departments, as indeed it is in some of them. I was interested in reading some comments on this very subject the other day in my home town paper, the Hamilton Spectator, in which it was said:
In fact the whole basis of present day government finance is the collection of revenue according to the individual's ability to pay and the spending of it according to the general interest of the nation.
I think we have ample evidence that this is true. The Spectator goes on to ask:
. . . why should Ottawa decide that just one department of government must be put on a paying basis -a department which performs a public service essential to the national good; a department which by increasing its charges can affect every citizen, raise the operating cost of every business and, quite possibly, interfere with that free communication which is vital to the development of a sprawling country.
The minister used as an argument the fact that it was not fair to ask the office girl or the worker or the little man to pay for the stamps of big firms like Eaton's, Morgan's, Simpson's and Dupuis Freres. That is precisely what they are doing, Mr. Speaker, under this new arrangement, because under the new rates these companies can claim the additional postage as an expense of doing business. For this reason it costs them less than 50 per cent of the additional postage because their taxes are in that category. The individual has no such advantage. What he pays out is a net loss to him. He is, in effect, therefore, doing that very thing, helping to pay for the postage of these companies which are, by reason of the nature of their operations, permitted to deduct from their cost of doing business the additional postage which they pay.
The little fellow who writes only a few letters each year is probably not in the income tax brackets. It is all very well to say this should be spread over all the people, but it is not spread over all the people. The little fellow now pays indirect taxation, sales taxes, and now the Post Office Department has decided he shall carry another levy which is not wholly paid by the industrial concerns of this country, the additional postage rate.
Later on, speaking of the four main proposals which he claimed the opposition had made, the minister said that if we should take the additional cost out of general taxes we should have a truly subsidized service. Towards the close of his remarks he said that this scheme would have illogical and dangerous consequences. Is this a new order under which we are operating? This is the

first evidence we have had that the government views with horror the idea of subsidization. Even granting the government has had a change of heart or that the Postmaster General stands alone in his new-found virtue, it must surely be admitted that, if the Post Office Department is not to have the benefit of subsidy, then by the same rule it should not be called upon to dispense gratuities to other departments of government from its revenue. As the Postmaster General reminded us yesterday, you cannot have your cake and eat it too.
It seems to me the minister also made a little play on what he referred to as "the elementary principle that one thing cannot at the same time be white and black". I think there was some reference to the sins of the opposition in regard thereto. It would appear that the opposition are not the only sinners, Mr. Speaker. Certainly the Postmaster General's remarks, and the inference being drawn from them, would indicate that the government is guilty in this regard, too. I was very much interested all the way through the statement which the Postmaster General made, and from time to time I made a few notes. Until I actually obtained the text of his statement, I am afraid that some of the implications escaped me. It is rather difficult to hear a statement read in the house and absorb the full implications at the time it is being given. I made a few notes which helped me in looking for what I considered to be the more interesting portions of the statement.
I should like to refer to one statement, which has already been mentioned briefly this afternoon by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace (Mr. Hamilton), and that concerns the financial picture revealed by the statements in the Postmaster General's annual report. The minister said the statements had been prepared for years along the same lines, and naturally are for comparative purposes. They do not furnish a financial picture along the lines that are usually provided in connection with commercial or industrial undertakings. Of course, that is apparent to even a casual observer.
The minister is basing his argument for an increase in rates on the figures of the department which he now admits do not reflect the true position; that is precisely what we have been saying right along. The minister is asking for an increase in rates which he cannot, under any circumstances, substantiate. Even today we had another example of this fact when several members of the government were unable to tell us just what the plans of the department and

the civil service commission were concerning the implementation of the five-day 40-hour week. If the Postmaster General and these other ministers have no idea just how the implementation is going to be effected, how can they say they need $5 million for this purpose? It is a guess, and probably a wild guess at that. I am amazed that, in the light of this, the minister has the temerity or possibly the naivete to ask this house to sanction an increase in postal rates because he feels that next year's fictitious figures will show a deficit. He does not know how much, but he comes to this house and asks for $15 million to play with, just in case we have a deficit.
The Postmaster General went on to make some other allegations. He related some of the things that we had said, and he said some things that we had not said. Speaking about the cost of operation of the department, he said that they had not calculated or taken into account the value of the services rendered to the department by the civil service commission. He went on to say what those services were. The same remark applied to the Department of Finance in connection with salary accounts, the writing of cheques and so on. He said these estimates do not take cognizance of the fact the Auditor General provides a free audit service. Do these departments not supply the same service to all other departments of government?
Let us follow this argument through to its logical conclusion. Supposing the Auditor General charged each department with the cost of auditing? I would think that by the time he got through at the end of the year there would be no need to have any estimates for the Auditor General's department, because all the other departments would have been charged with those costs. In turn, each of the departments preparing its estimates would put in an item for auditing. They do not do that. Apparently the Postmaster General thinks they should. Supposing the Department of Finance charged each other department of government with expenses in connection with salary services. In that case, the estimates of the Department of Finance would be materially reduced. All of these arguments which the minister used merely serve to point out our main contention, that the department itself does not know where it stands; yet it asks for an increase in rates.
The minister also tried to link up remarks which had been made by my leader with a reference to the situation in the United States. After telling that a speech had been made by the President of the United States, 83276-116

in which he intimated his intention to ask for an increase in postal rates, and despite the fact that this matter has not been considered by the congress of the United States, he said:
This makes it clear that the United States government is abandoning the policy which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) suggests we should follow.
Mr. Speaker, a little marginal note I made yesterday when the minister made this statement is, I fear, distinctly unparliamentary. So, following his example, I suppose I should make that confession, and then withdraw the unspoken remark, as he did yesterday.

I do not want to be sued. The very idea of suggesting that in our opposition to the increase we are likely to build up a deficit of $770 million, or even the Canadian equivalent, on a per capita basis, of about $55 million, is simply ridiculous. Apparently the minister and his advisers know this full well, because otherwise I fancy they would be asking for an 8-cent mail rate instead of a 5-cent rate. And that is just about what would be needed to cover a deficit of $55 million.
We contend that the 5-cent rate now proposed is just as unnecessary as an 8-cent rate would be, and we say the government has yet to show good and sufficient reasons why this essential service should not be supplied to the people of Canada at rates which are now in effect.
The Postmaster General then went on to talk about the cost of making the alterations in the service which had been suggested by the J. D. Woods and Gordon report. He admonished the house to please bear this increase in mind.
Well, Mr. Speaker, expert business consultants do not suggest expenditures unless they can justify those expenditures in subsequent savings and increased efficiency- and probably both. And so to say that the cost of making these improvements is something which should be borne in mind is unrealistic. What we want to know is not what it will cost to put the improvements into effect, but what the saving will be to the department if the improvements are put into effect.
And then in glowing terms the minister painted the picture of the wonderful administration the department had enjoyed over the years. In fact he took so long to do it that the little note I wrote yesterday I am going to repeat today, and it was simply this: The gentleman doth protest too much,

Post Office Act
methinks. I know the minister thinks his department is pretty good, but I doubt if he thinks it is so good that it can claim credit for the increase in the volume of mail, which undoubtedly bears some relationship to the increase in population. After all, the increase in the volume of mail handled should have some staff advantages, particularly at the administrative level. While it may take two postmen to carry twice as much mail, it certainly does not take two postmasters to supervise it. And with that increase in volume there is bound to be a saving in overhead at the administrative level.
So I cannot really believe that the Postmaster General gave too much thought to his statement that the increase in volume of mail by 178 per cent, and in staff by only 100 per cent, was a great achievement and I suggest that his bragging was not very well based. I am sure anyone who has been actively engaged in industry would not think it was much of a boast.
Then he went on to say that the officials of the department, entirely without any help, had replaced the old system of handling money order accounts. Well, I presume he was referring to the system of punched card accounting which they adopted. I must say that it is very laudable to find that this modern system was put into effect. But that is only ordinary business practice. It is used by all sorts of industries and by governments where large volume passes through their hands, and where such a change would make the procedure more efficient so that it would pay for itself.
But here again he brags about the amount that has been saved, and gives the figure of $350,000. I do not doubt that at all. But if by keeping up with improved accounting methods the department can save $350,000 annually in just one operation, how much can it save if it follows the recommendation in the Woods-Gordon report that modern techniques in materials handling be adopted? We do not know the answer to that. We know it is in the report, but we do not know what could be saved.
The minister says that we cannot make sufficient savings to keep the postage rate where it is today, but how does he know that is so? He admits a saving of a third of a million dollars in one operation. In one breath he says no great savings can be made and in the next he boasts of what he has done in adopting modern methods. How inconsistent can you get? The more I read the minister's statement, the more amazed I became.

Then, going on to speak about savings, he said that in the report they do not at any point indicate that these savings are to be realized immediately. Of course, you do not realize savings immediately when you change over your system. It stands to reason that it takes time to put in new methods and to introduce new techniques. It may even cost a little more until you get your new machinery, your new equipment and new system in full operation. But eventually you will make money on it, and save.
He has said it may be several months before the changes are finally completed. Well if he anticipates that it will be several months before these changes are completed, and if he admits that he has already saved over a third of a million dollars on one change, and if he also admits that this report has made suggestions which the department is seriously considering and which he hopes to put into effect, then why raise the rates now? Why not wait? Why not wait to see what can be done? After all, the department has had deficits before. It would not be the first time it has operated on a deficit.
The whole point is that he is estimating a deficit of which he is not sure-and I maintain he could not even hope to substantiate that estimate later on. Yet he asks for an increase in the postage rate at a time when he has no idea of what the results of operations may be in the department, under new and modernized conditions. Then he said:
Thus the sweeping statements to the effect that efficient administration will permit us to make enough savings to meet the added cost are swept away by the facts.
What facts? The fact that you can save and have saved $350,000 in one operation? Does that prove that the minister cannot make a saving? I think it proves quite the reverse. Then he goes on to the question of franking, and he says that the suggested abolition of franking would cover only a small fraction of the total additional expenditures of $13,500,000, and calls this just another futile suggestion which brings no remedy to the situation.
Well, Mr. Speaker, as I recall it, the amount which the department itself estimates as being lost through franking is very close to $5 million. I believe the exact figure was $4,700,000. That is well over a third of the additional expense which the Postmaster General anticipates, and upon which he is basing his request for a 1-cent increase in the rates.
He goes on to say that the principle of franking is to give free mail communication

to those seeking, as well as to those supplying, administrative information. We know all that. And then he says the privilege is given so that free mail communication may be established between the Canadian public, the ministers and members of parliament. As I recall it, we mentioned the matter of franking, but not only the mail and communications which flow between constituents and their members and ministers. We mentioned also that this practice is indulged in rather promiscuously, if I may say so, by the various departments of government.
Who suggested in this house that franking should be abolished? As I recall it, it was the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) who mentioned it. Later on the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) suggested it. I think it is only natural that other hon. members in different parts of the house should then take up the cry. As I pointed out during the resolution stage, there is much useless mail from departmental sources. I should like to read to the house a communication I received which I think well points up this claim. This letter came to me with its enclosure a week ago, after the debate on the resolution stage. It is addressed from the Norberry school, St. Vital, Manitoba, under date of January 19, 1954, and the text is as follows:
Recently I noted that you spoke out against the proposed increase in postal rates. I too am opposed. I believe that considerable saving could be achieved at the government level. As proof I forward the enclosed book.
The book is the Canadian record of performance for purebred dairy cattle, Jersey.
Weekly, similar material arrives from the Department of Agriculture. This is an elementary and junior high school in suburban Winnipeg.
There may be some citizens who would be interested and even excited to discover that Fancy Girl, whose sire was Basil, gave milk for 305 days amounting to 3841 pounds of which 5-7 per cent was butterfat. However the teachers and pupils of this school do not seem to be included in this number. Doubtless they haven't been properly orientated or activated or whatever the word is that the progressive educationalists would use.
However this is only the record of the Jersey cows. You must know that there are other branches of the cow family and that their numbers are even more numerous, necessitating thicker and heavier books.
To date I haven't been able to discover any possible use for such material. However I could- and this is a fiendish idea-select some particularly recalcitrant boys and as punishment have them figure out which cow averaged the most pounds of milk per milking day. That ought to settle their hash. However I would run afoul of the Geneva convention.
More seriously, this information must be compiled at considerable expense to the taxpayer. Surely this expense could be reduced by producing only sufficient copies to satisfy a carefully-selected mailing 83276-1164
Post Office Act
list. Those who desire such information must be highly specialized and would request it. To have postmen going about the country delivering this information to institutions and individuals who have no recourse but to consign it to the wastepaper basket, is a senseless waste of public monies.
Yours truly,
V. H. L. Wyatt, Principal.
When I made my remarks at the resolution stage, I did not have a specimen at hand. At that time I said that much of the material which comes across our desks bearing the government frank is pure junk. I do not mean that this particular report is pure junk, but in so far as this recipient is concerned it is just that. If the recipient has no use for it, why have it printed and why have it sent out? Then why turn around and say to the taxpayers of this country, "We shall have to charge another cent for first-class mail because the Post Office Department is losing money". It is perfectly ridiculous.
In speaking of the franking privilege, far from saying that the privilege itself should be abolished, I said that the Post Office Department should receive credit from the other departments of government to which mail service was supplied. This is not a matter of abolishing the franking privilege, it is simply a bookkeeping matter. If the taxpayer has the right to free mail, he certainly has the right to cheap mail. To say on the one hand that you must not abolish his franking privilege and on the other hand to say to him that he has to put another cent on every letter he writes unless he writes it to the government or to his member of parliament is pure nonsense.

When we put the full onus of that increase on the general public it is the same as adding additional taxes to the goods they have to purchase: When we add an increase in first-class mail rates it affects every human being in this dominion.
In my view the attempt to raise money in that fashion demonstrates that no thought whatsoever has been given to means of raising the money from those who can best afford to pay. The minister surely would not argue for a moment that those in the low income brackets, in the exceedingly low income brackets, can afford to pay any more than they are paying now. Yet under this bill the minister is going to do just that very thing. '
It seems to me that he should have looked around for some other means to raise that money, if it were necessary; and I am not so sure that it is necessary. For instance, with regard to our second-class mail, we subsidize newspapers to the extent of $10 million every year. The amount used to be $12 million. CURRENCY, MINT AND EXCHANGE FUND ACT AMENDMENT TO PERMIT MINTING AND MARKETING OP GOLD COINS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 173, to amend the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in his place and to welcome him back from Australia.
This act would, in fact, establish a free market for gold within Canada. It would establish a free market for gold in a country

which is not resorting to the evils of exchange control, currency restriction or any of the other trade-destroying measures that have been developed by money managers, in central governments and in the central banks since the war, and in many cases long before that. The bill sets out and describes a coin which is designated as to weight and fineness only. The fineness is 900 and the weight of pure gold contained in the coin is one troy ounce. It is similar in the amount of gold it contains to the gold coin now being minted by the firm of Rothschild and Company and put out under the name of the First Banking Corporation of Tangier. I say it is similar in weight of gold. It differs in fineness, the fineness of the Tangier coin being 916-7, which is rather greater. The coin would of course bear a Canadian insignia. The first point I wish to make, before I discuss some of my reasons for introducing the measure, is that today under our strange so-called free marketing of gold, which is certainly not free marketing in the true sense, Canadian gold from our largest single gold producer and all our base metal mines is shipped through some recognized broker to Paris or some other market, but chiefly Paris, I believe, where it is sold to somebody else. As a matter of fact I was informed that the few coins I was able to secure were actually Canadian gold shipped, refined and sold through the Rothschild organization.
It seems a great pity to me that Canadian gold should leave Canada in this form. If it were minted into a convenient coin, which I have endeavoured to describe, a great deal of it would remain in Canada. A great deal of it would be purchased by individuals and corporations, and under the terms of the bill it could be purchased by the Bank of Canada or any other designated agency, but they would have to bid for it on an open exchange. Therefore most of the gold at least would not be lost to Canada, as it is under our present marketing system.
I suggest that would be a great advantage. While I have inserted a clause in the bill whereby its importation or exportation shall be free, because I think that is essential in the establishment of any free market, nevertheless a great deal of it would remain here to be put to useful purposes rather than lost in the international sea. In addition, from what reports we have been able to obtain recently, the uses to which it is being put are inimical to the well-being of the western democracies. So much for the first point.
The second point, on which I wish to speak a little later at some length, has to do with
Proposed Minting of Gold Coins how we would know what the price would be. That is exactly the point which I consider to be important. Would the price be greater or less than $35? Frequently, when I have made these suggestions, people have asked me whether, if the Americans withdrew their guarantee to purchase all gold at $35 an ounce, they would dump gold on the market and depress the price. The only answer I have to that is to ask whether, if an individual, a corporation or a nation has an asset for which it has paid a certain price, would it be willing, in order to depress the price of the asset it has bought, to dump it on the free markets of the world.
Would the United States government, for instance, in order to depress the price of zinc, lead or copper, initiate a program of dumping their stockpiles of these metals on the already jittery base metal markets? Surely an operation such as that cannot be contemplated by any reasonable individual. They have bought these stockpiles of zinc, copper and lead. Are they prepared to dump these metals on the markets in order to depress the price? In my opinion, despite the fact that the zinc, lead and copper were bought for strategic uses, they would be no more likely to dump their stockpiles of these metals than they would dump their stockpile of gold. First of all, they would be destroying a United States government asset. They would have paid $35 an ounce for so many million ounces of gold. If they dumped it at $30 an ounce there would be a net loss to the United States of so many dollars an ounce, the amount varying in proportion to the price under $35 at which the gold was sold.
Now, it is said that Russia has resorted to these tactics. All I can say to that, Mr. Speaker, is that although we have no accurate figures, Russia is probably the second largest gold producer in the world. Her gold production has been estimated-although I give no credence to these figures-at some $200 million per annum at $35 per ounce. Not only has Russia been a major producer of gold but she has been able, through conquest, to get the gold hoards in the national treasuries of the countries she has overrun, like Roumania, Czechoslovakia, Poland, the Baltic countries, and possibly others. It is quite likely, therefore, that Russia has a considerable hoard of gold.
Apparently the new Malenkov policy in Russia is to ease the lot of the long suffering people by making what are known as consumer goods and food a little more plentiful. In order to accomplish this, and because of the failure of her collective farms, she has had to buy large amounts of food outside her national boundaries. Apparently the only
