Proposed Minting of Gold Coins medium of exchange was gold. A few years ago when gold was selling at $45 and $50 per ounce on the free market, I was surprised that Russia did not undertake the action she has taken today. I feel that the reason was internal Russian politics. I do know that for a time she was buying machinery of the most strategic sort in Switzerland. As a matter of fact, there was a delicate international situation in Europe because Russia was able to buy machine tools and other tools in France, Switzerland and elsewhere and, by devious means, get them back into Russia. I believe that has been largely stopped by international action by the western democracies.
So much for the fear that the United States will dump gold in order to destroy the $35 price. It is unrealistic, because in all my life I have never seen a Yankee who was prepared to throw away money he had spent in purchasing something. We come again to what the price would be on the free market. I suggest that the price is unimportant. It is not the price which is so important, but the stability of that price; and that is something which is extremely difficult to arrive at. The only true method by which a stable price can be arrived at is through open market transactions. If you peg the price of any commodity it leads either to surpluses or to chaotic market conditions. Shortly I propose to mention what the Randall commission said on that very point in the report released just a week ago.
We want the gold to perform a useful function. At the present time gold is taken from the producing mines in Canada under extremely difficult conditions. I ask hon. members what product could be sold today for 10 per cent less than in 1939 and have the industry producing that product still in existence. The fact that we have a gold industry is nothing short of a miracle. With the exception of three or four mines, the existence of the industry is entirely dependent upon the benevolence of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act and the Canadian taxpayers.
I believe that is a most unfortunate situation. What the costs of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act this year will be, I do not know. The strike situation has upset things, so we do not know how much it will cost, but it is assumed it will cost in the neighbourhood of $15 million. Now, the money of the taxpayers of Canada is just keeping the gold mining industry alive today.
I believe it is money well spent, because if that industry ceased to exist for any reason a whole series of northern municipalities would also cease to exist and would become ghost towns; and in an expanding country


like Canada, we cannot contemplate the closing down of our northern frontier. But the principle is wrong; the principle of bonusing any industry, to keep it in existence, is wrong. Neither I in this House of Commons nor, so far as I know, any of the major gold mines, or the gold industry as a whole, recommended this form of subsidy to keep the industry in existence, when the legislation was first introduced.
The mines that ship on the free market are prepared to do so without this subsidy. I have not consulted with or talked to any of my mining friends with regard to this proposed legislation, but if a free market could be established in Canada I feel sure that within a comparatively short space of time the money we are spending on the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act might be saved to the Canadian people. I admit that, compared with a gross national product valued at $25 billion, this $15 million is not a very great sum. But even $15 million is certainly not hay.
Consider the problem of marketing gold under the present situation. By no stretch of the imagination can this be called a free market, nor can it be so considered. What happens is that the mine, submitting bullion to a broker, says, "We have so much to submit". The broker asks at what price it is offered. It is not a bid-and-asked proposition as in normal stock exchange procedure. It is a one-way procedure; the mine takes it or leaves it; the price is set. The gold must be exported. It leaves the country, and the mine has no further say in its disposition once it passes into the hands of the broker.
I feel that this is delivering the mining industry into the hands of brokers, and I think that is a wrong procedure. It is bad in principle. I congratulate the government upon the fact that the mines may now sell fine gold without having to go through the ridiculous process of adulterating it and then having it re-refined when it hits the European market. It is marketed in countries the economies of which, to say the least, are not too stable.
A friend of mine asked me this question the other day. If you have a bearer bond or a Canada savings bond, which is a pretty good security, would you be very happy to have it in a safety deposit box in Paris or Tangier, or would you sooner have it in your own box at home? It seems to me that is a pretty good argument for the ownership of gold. If a corporation has a few thousand ounces of gold, where would they like to keep or to store it? Surely it would be in a country with a stable form of government

and with a stable economy. Surely they would like to store that gold either in Canada or the United States.
To preclude that is, I think, wrong. That is the question I put before the house in connection with the holding and ownership of gold. Gold held in a country whose economy is safe and stable is likely to be much more valuable than gold held in a country the economy of which is not safe, and whose future is anything but secure. It goes without saying that if one has a painting of one of the old masters he would sooner have it here in Canada than leave it in some country in which there might be a revolution at any time.
So I suggest it is reasonable to expect that if gold were sold within the confines of a country which, first of all, is not practising exchange control, and second is at peace and is geographically situated away from centres of strife and turmoil, a country possessing a buoyant economy and a stable form of government, it would increase in value.
So much for the price of gold. But, as I have said, the price is not the important thing. The important thing is, first of all, the usefulness to which that gold can be put and, second, the availability of the metal.
I have mentioned the Randall report. I have not read it in detail because it contains well over a hundred pages of closely written script. One of the points the Randall commission makes, to my mind one of the most important points, is the futility of trying to peg and to control the market price of any commodity. It takes issue, for instance, with the international wheat agreement. It takes issue with all schemes whereby an artificial price for a commodity is aimed at. With that I must say I am in entire agreement.
Any attempt to peg the price of copper, lead, zinc, aluminum, wheat, cotton or any commodity at a level above or below the world market price, that is the price you can get for it on the open market, is doomed to disaster. All such devices as the bill to restrict the importation of Canadian base metals into the United States, which fortunately has not been proceeded with, are doomed to failure. They may succeed for a time by the device of parity prices, by providing artificial price support; but by creating a high-level economy and a high-priced end product they can do nothing in the long run but destroy the world market for the particular product.
What is the harm in allowing people to own gold? What is wrong with it? First of all, gold is not like uranium. It is not fissionable. You cannot blow anything up with it.
Proposed Minting of Gold Coins You cannot make a bomb of it. You cannot make a narcotic of it. You cannot smoke it, You cannot injure anybody with it. Why have we in Canada denied to our citizens the right to hold and own gold? Surely it can only be the restrictions of the international monetary fund.

speechtext:
I am glad to know there were so many happy and foolish people down there. Has the international monetary

Proposed Minting of Gold Coins fund assisted in the convertibility of currencies? Are our currencies any more convertible today than they were at that time? Unfortunately the answer is no. Why? Because the rules set up by the fund made most difficult the convertibility of soft currencies, sterling currencies, into the so-called hard currencies.
What has been the reason? The reason has simply been that the soft currencies, which are designated as currencies which bear no relationship to gold, have been unable to be converted into hard currencies through the common denominator of gold. So no matter how the restrictions were framed they have proved of great disservice to us as a trading nation, and they have not assisted the trading of the world. This is simply because the price of gold was set and the ownership and holding of it by individuals was not allowed.
With gold, purchases can be made anywhere in the world. The Russians have proved that, the Swiss have proved that, and anyone who has travelled in the Levant in recent years knows that to be so. Through the operation of this fund we have virtually sterilized gold and made it not a useful commodity but merely a metal to be taken from one hole in the ground and put in another, there to remain inert. So much for what has happened with regard to the convertibility of currencies.
There are hard currencies, which theoretically have some relationship to gold, and there are soft currencies which apparently do not. In between them you have this great impasse, this great gulf of lack of convertibility simply because the problem, the correct equation and the proper use of gold, has not been solved.
My suggestions have met with considerable approval. The town of Timmins, for example, passed a resolution which I imagine was forwarded to the minister, in which they recommended the minting of gold coins. In that resolution they used an argument which I think is valid. The resolution states:
While the government is not in a position to have the price of gold increased, it can increase its use.
The mayor of Timmins stated, and I think this also is a valid argument, that it was time gold was freed from the restrictions placed on it by the international monetary fund. Outside of uranium it was the only metal so treated, he said. What is the danger in increasing the use of gold in Canada? What harm can it do? Can it upset world trade? Surely if we have a free market for gold in Canada it becomes possible to pay those people who sell to us in gold. They can be paid in gold through devious channels


today, but with a free market the transaction would be automatic and government agencies would not require to be consulted.
Another advantage is that people coming to Canada would be able to obtain gold for their ordinary business transactions, and it would also assist persons doing business with Canada. For example, people with insurance policies in a Canadian company would be offered the choice of having their claims met in gold at the daily rate for which gold was being offered.
I would now like to quote a paragraph from an article by an economist I believe in, Henry Hazlitt. In the fourth of his articles on this question he states, and I am quoting from the issue of Newsweek dated January 25, 1954:
A full gold-coin standard is desirable because a gold-bullion standard is merely a rich man's standard. A relatively poor man should be just as able to protect himself against inflation, to the extent of his dollar holdings, as a rich man. The reason for returning to a full gold-coin standard in several stages is to prevent too sudden a drain on gold reserves before confidence has been reestablished. A program like the foregoing would provide a faster schedule.
In the earlier part of his article he sets out a timetable for the return to a full gold standard; and a free gold market is the first stage.
Let us assume this market was established. The average individual, who is always forgotten today, would have the right to own-gold coins, export them, import them, or do whatever he wished with them. Thus, if further inflation occurred he would be able, through the ownership of gold, to protect himself against it. That is a very important point, because obviously we are passing from the lush years of the seller's market into extremely combative years when our goods will have to be sold under conditions of the keenest competition. It may be that if the unemployment situation becomes acute this government, as well as the government of the United States, will have to resort to deficit financing. I hope it does not come to that, but I am certain it will if the unemployment situation grows.
Deficit financing by any other term means inflation. It means the government issues more money than it collects. Under such conditions the ownership of gold would protect the individual, particularly the poor man. The man of means, the man of wealth, can protect himself by the ownership of real estate, common stocks, or real property, but the man with a comparatively small income is denied such protection. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that is the essential fifth freedom

which we and all the democracies seem to have forgotten, namely the right of the individual to protect himself against the results of arbitrary action by the central government.
Such protection is imperative. Freedom of religion, freedom of trade, freedom of worship and the other freedoms are actually part of the total freedom, which is the economic freedom which can only be provided through the ownership of gold.
If we do not do something like this, if we continue our present policy, we shall be faced with the complete decay of the gold mining industry. We are faced with the loss of our gold into the hands of those who can use it for purposes which are inimical to our welfare. I am told that a considerable amount of the rioting and the assassinating which is taking place in the Arab countries has been financed by gold. That is hardly a use to which I should like to see Canadian gold put.
As I say, we leave our northern municipalities and our mining industry at the mercy of brokers who are not interested in the welfare of Canada. We thus lose a priceless asset. At the same time we continue, under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, the expenditure of some $15 million a year, money which could be saved. We have not approached any closer to the solution of the question of convertibility of currencies. Instead of being a useful adjunct to our economy, the gold is either used against us or is sterilized. Neither course is desirable.
I have spoken at some length on this question this afternoon, Mr. Speaker. I wished as far as possible to speak without notes or a prepared script because I wanted, if possible, to explain to the hon. members of this house why I feel that our present course not only is not assisting the industry or the northern municipalities, important as they are, but is not assisting Canada as a trading nation.
I cannot see any danger in allowing gold to be traded freely in Canada. I cannot see that the ownership of gold by Canadians can do anyone any harm. On the other hand I can see that, through the free ownership of gold, you are going to provide for many Canadians a form of security against further inflation, and are going to allow them to maintain, through the holding of gold, the ownership of a tangible, finite substance, something which throughout the centuries has maintained its value and commanded a price. It is not gold which has shrunk in price. It is not gold nor the gold standard which has failed. What has failed is the belief that those money managers in central governments and central
Proposed Minting of Gold Coins banks can control world prices for products and for their currencies. This has never been done successfully, although it has been done at times over periods of years. However, it has always proved to be a disaster.
For this reason I would ask that this bill be given consideration. What harm does it do? Who does it help? Will it not assist in the convertibility of currencies? Will it not aid Canada as a great international trading nation? It is on this basis that I put forward this amendment to the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act.

It has already been made crystal clear from this side of the house, Mr. Speaker, that we are opposed to the increase in postage rates involved in the bill which has been brought in by the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote). I shall, therefore, take only a moment or two to deal directly with that point. However, there is a particular aspect of this matter about which I want to say something further.
With regard to the increase in the postage rate itself, I feel that the government has not played fair with the Canadian people. In that respect I feel that the blame should be levelled not so much at the Postmaster General personally as at the government. I think perhaps he has had to take rather too much of the blame for this on behalf of the government as a whole.
The first of the two main ways in which the government has not played fair with the Canadian people is its action in taking off a tax just before the election and putting it on again just after the election, under another name. The second way in which I feel the government is not playing fair with the people of the country has to do with the

fact that nothing is being said on the government side of the house in reply to the many speeches from this side in which reference has been made to the losses being sustained by the post office in respect of periodicals and magazines. I refer in particular to those which carry huge amounts of advertising, which means that the Post Office Department is subsidizing periodicals, newspapers and magazines that are making a considerable revenue out of that advertising. These publications are carried at a tremendous loss to the post office, so far as postage is concerned.
I give the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) credit for attempting to answer-though I do not feel he has answered satisfactorily-a number of the arguments put forward from this side of the house. Unless something has happened that has escaped my observation, I have not yet heard him deal with this question, to which I have now once more drawn attention. If my study of the matter has served me correctly, the deficit which the Postmaster General says must be met could be made up if magazines, periodicals and newspapers were made to pay their share of what it costs the Post Office Department to transmit this material. And the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) reminds me, from the back of the chamber, that if that were done there would be, in relation to the deficit the Postmaster General is now talking about, a surplus of $2,500,000.
So I submit that this is more than just a protest in the name of the Canadian people aeainst a one-cent increase in postage rates. Naturally people do not like increases in taxes of any kind. Protest against an increase would be natural in any case. But I feel this is something more; it is a case of the government not playing fair with the people of Canada in respect of this matter. And I think it is quite appropriate that my leader has moved that the bill be given the six months' hoist. That is what this parliament should do with it, hoist it out of the House of Commons altogether.
The bill was introduced by the Postmaster General with a speech in which he said specifically that one of its purposes is to make up for the cost of the five-day 40-hour week, which is to be implemented on April 1. We have heard that statement on at least three occasions from the Postmaster General. We had it when he introduced the resolution preceding the bill; we had it again when he moved second reading, and we also had it from another minister on December 8, 1953, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) announced that in due course there would be this bill increasing the rates of postage.

On each of those occasions reference has been made to the fact that one of the reasons for the bill is the need to raise $5 million, the cost of implementing the five-day 40-hour week. For a while I took it as a matter of course that it would take some time for the government to work out the details in connection with the implementation of the five-day 40-hour week. For a while I kept my suspicious nature under control; but as time goes on I am finding that more difficult.
It is now nearly two months since, on December 8, 1953, as recorded at pages 692 and 693 of Hansard, the Minister of Finance told me he hoped that very shortly there would be made public a list of the localities in which the post office staffs would go on the five-day 40-hour week on April 1. I had hoped that that list would be published very shortly. Maybe my definition of "shortly" varies from that of the minister; but at any rate on January 14, 1954, as recorded at page 1139 of Hansard I asked the Postmaster General if that list was yet ready, and he had to tell me that it was not.
I waited a little while longer. Yesterday, February 4, 1954, as recorded at page 1762 of Hansard, I asked again if we might soon have information particularly with respect to the manipulative staffs working in the post office at Winnipeg. Again I was told that this information was not yet available.
Well, today, as Your Honour will recall, I asked the question again, this time putting it to the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill), the minister responsible to parliament for the civil service commission. I happen to know that others have been trying to ascertain from the civil service commission whether or not certain cities, certain communities in the country, are to be included in the five-day 40-hour week arrangement. Up to the present time we have been unable to get any information in answer to that question, except the one bit of information which the Minister of Finance was able to give this afternoon when I raised the question of privilege. The information he gave to the house was something like this, that if the member for Winnipeg North Centre was concerned about his city, he could be assured that Winnipeg would be included.
Well, it will be a matter of some relief to the post office employees in Winnipeg to know that their case is covered. But it seems to me that it is not fair to the house as a whole not to give us the complete information as to the extent to which the five-day 40-hour week is to be implemented. We have been led to believe that it is the civil service commission which works out these matters. We
Post Office Act
found out this afternoon from the Minister of Finance that the personnel side of treasury board is working on it as well. But no one knows what the list of communities is.
This afternoon, however, the Minister of Finance was able to assure me that Winnipeg is on the list. Well, either he is jumping the gun, or he knows the communities that are on that list; and if he does, then I submit that before the house is asked to give second reading to the bill we should have that information. It is not fair to ask us in advance of that information to pass a bill which would provide money for that purpose. What position are we going to be in after the bill is passed by the house-if it is passed-if we find that the implementation of the five-day 40-hour week does not measure up to what we thought would be the case, with the proposed expenditure of $5 million?
I want to know what the situation is in some other cities. Is it going to be extended to Regina and Saskatoon? What about a large city like Montreal? Is the five-day week already sufficiently established in that city that one could be assured post office staffs there will be included; or are we going to have the experience, after this goes through and after the postal rate has been increased for this, among other purposes, of learning that a city like Montreal is not included?
I suppose members from every city in the country could rise on questions of privilege, as I did this afternoon, and worm information out of the Minister of Finance. But surely that is not the proper way to do it. As a member from Winnipeg I was glad to get that information this afternoon for the employees in my city. But I submit it is not fair to the house as a whole to ask us to go on without having complete information.
Just when the debate on second reading will be concluded, I do not know. Certainly there is no possibility of the matter being finally concluded tonight, so far as third reading is concerned, because it would require unanimous consent to go to third reading tonight. In other words I think it should be clear that since there is further time beyond today the government should play fair with the house, even if it is not playing fair with the Canadian people in the matter of raising these postal rates, by seeing to it that this list of communities and localities where the five-day 40-hour week is to go into effect is before this house before we go any further.
From what the minister said this afternoon we know that Winnipeg is one community that is on the list. That is fine, but

let us have the entire list before we go any further. It is two months since the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said the list would be ready very shortly. I hope the period regarded as "very shortly" has now gone by, even when considered in the minister's terms.
Some of us do not accept the proposition that there is necessarily a connection between the cost of the five-day 40-hour week and the postal rates. Other civil servants have been given the five-day 40-hour week without the Canadian people having imposed upon them a special tax for that purpose. But the government has taken the position that there is a connection in this case. All right; if from the government's viewpoint there is a connection, then I submit we are entitled to full information on that point before we go any further with this obnoxious legislation.

Mr. Speaker, in rising for a moment to oppose this increase to five cents in the postal rate for first-class mail I wish to say that I do so because of the many protests I have received from my own riding.
The Postmaster General has said that this is the only way in which the increased costs of the department can be met. Postal delivery is a service which the taxpaying public has a right to expect the government to provide, and that public does not necessarily expect that the department which provides this service shall be self-sustaining. Quite apart from being self-sustaining, in the past few years it has been profit-producing.
I presume that those profits have gone into the general revenues of the government and have been used for other services which the government provides for the people of this country. Therefore I see no reason at all why the government should be in such a rush to offset any possibility of loss in the department by increasing rates before they have found out whether or not they are going to need the extra revenue.
Certainly the government does not take this attitude with regard to Canadian National Railways. Most certainly it does not take this attitude in connection with Trans-Canada Air Lines, and certainly not with regard to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. As a matter of fact, so far as T.C.A. is concerned the Post Office Department was called upon to accept a rather heavy charge for first-class mail, which might very well be described as a subsidy to T.C.A. which prior to that time had not been doing so well financially.
Over a period of ten years the surpluses of the Post Office Department amounted to

$70,193,330.54 and for the preceding ten years the surpluses were $22,969,606.69, making a total of more than $90 million of a surplus in the last 20 years in the operations of this department. And this was at the lower stamp rates which were in effect during that period of time.
I know from correspondence which I have had with different groups in my riding that this increase certainly is not popular. Personally I simply cannot understand why this government is advancing the rate to five cents on first-class mail. To me the raising of the rate to five cents from the three-cent rate which prevailed before the war-and at the present time it is only three cents in the United States-simply does not make sense.

Mr. Speaker, during the course of this debate we have heard a great deal about the advantages the new air mail service which is to come with the proposed increased rates will bring to parts of Canada such as the Yukon, Newfoundland and elsewhere. But it seems to me that the question should be raised here as to what advantages are going to accrue to some of the older parts of Canada.
In Ontario and Quebec there are a great manv people living on the sideroads in rural areas. These people live on farms which have been well established and settled for many generations. In some cases they still have to go half a mile or a mile to get their mail during the winter.
Since the end of the war there has been a great influx of immigrants and a considerable increase in our population. Many new subdivisions have been developed outside of a number of our medium-sized cities. This condition is to be found throughout western Ontario. As I say, these subdivisions in many cases are not within the city limits and therefore do not receive daily mail delivery. Quite often you will find 20 or 30 houses on a side-road with 20 or 30 mail boxes down at the end of that road. Those people have to go down to collect their mail, sometimes having to travel half a mile or so.
I cannot see how the new postal rates are going to bring any great advantage to those people. It is alleged that the people who use the service should pay for it. These people will be using first-class mail, yet they will gain no advantages from the increased rates, while the people in some of the newer parts of Canada will gain considerable advantage. That does not seem to me to be reasonable.
During this debate we have had a multiplicity of figures given as to why there should or should not be an increase in the postal rates. The minister has given some figures,

as have hon. members of the opposition. From the reports which we have it would appear that in each of the years 1951, 1952 and 1953 the Post Office Department had a surplus of about $6 million. The minister has estimated that there will be a loss of around $7,500,000 this year because of the elimination of the stamps on cheques.
The Woods-Gordon report recommends many savings that could be effected within the department if certain economies were put into effect. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) has suggested that the people who are going to pay this increased first-class rate are going to pay more than their share. We all know that from an accounting point of view it is quite possible to adopt various viewpoints. For instance, we all know that it is perfectly proper accounting practice to value fixed assets in different ways, to allocate costs in different ways and so on. I mention that in passing merely to show that often it is quite possible to show a profit or to show a loss if one so desires.
It would seem that the minister is not too sure what are the receipts and expenditures of the Post Office Department. For instance, last spring the minister's predecessor apparently felt the revenue was sufficient so that the tax on cheques was no longer necessary, and that tax was accordingly removed.
This fall we have the situation that the hon. minister has changed his mind again, and it is necessary now to increase postal rates to make up the deficit. Surely between last spring and last fall the figures of estimates and expenditures would have been available to the minister. If not, then it is quite possible on that basis that by the coming spring we will have no need to increase the rates at all.
In view of the fact that last spring the department took off a tax because it was not considered necessary, and then this fall it put on another tax because a certain amount of revenue is now considered necessary, and in view of other figures we have had presented from all sides of the house, which are most confusing, it would seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that the correct thing to do would be to wait and see. It may be that by the end of this year it will not be necessary to raise the postal rates. In fact it would seem, from all we have heard, that it would be entirely unnecessary to raise the rates. In any event, should there be a deficit at the end of this year the minister could always bring in this bill again and increase the rates next year if necessary.
As the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) pointed out earlier today, the removal of the stamp tax on cheques certainly
Post Office Act
benefited large businesses, and there is no doubt that the increase in the postage rate will certainly affect those with small incomes who cannot deduct such charges as expenses.
In closing these brief remarks, Mr. Speaker, I think I should emphasize once again that the policy of wait and see should be adopted at the present time and this tax introduced at a later date when it is proved to be necessary.

Mr. Speaker, although there have been some very critical remarks regarding the postal service, I believe it is remarkable that we have as good a postal service as we now enjoy when we consider some of the handicaps which have been mentioned during this debate.
Last night I received a letter from an 86-vear-old friend of mine which was posted in Edmonton at 7.30 p.m. on February 3. By 7.00 p.m. Edmonton time on the 4th of February it was on my desk. The writer of this letter settled in Saskatchewan 50 years ago. It is quite remarkable that during his lifetime he should be in a position to post a letter in Edmonton one day and have it delivered here in Ottawa in less than 24 hours.
Having said that, however, I must say that I am supporting the amendment moved by the leader of this group. I want to emphasize what has been said by several members on this side of the house, namely that first-class mail is being operated, according to figures issued a year ago, at a profit of $20,700,000, and on the other hand second-class mail for some years has been losing 13J cents out of every dollar, or a total loss of $16 million.
When one considers that that subsidy has been a factor in building up some of the immense fortunes made in the newspaper field I believe the government is not really being fair with the Canadian people in leaving the rates on that class of mail unchanged. In this connection, and to demonstrate my point, I need only mention the Thomson syndicate which operates not only in Canada but which recently bought the Scotsman in Edinburgh for several million dollars last year; the Southam group; the Toronto Star; the Toronto Globe and Mail; the Sifton group; and the hon. member of the Senate who died recently leaving $1,750,000. I do not know how much of that was made in the newspaper business, but he certainly did not lose anything in that field.
When these large fortunes have been made partly through the advantage accruing from the very low cost of second-class mail, I think the government has no right to place this tax on the Canadian people by increasing the letter rate by one cent.

The next point I want to deal with, and it has not been dealt with adequately, is the action of Liberal candidates in dragging the affairs of the Post Office Department into politics. I received a letter from a Mr. John Fletcher of Kelvington and in this letter dated January 12, 1954 he enclosed a clipping from a local newspaper. That report states there is an item in the estimates of $110,000 for a new post office building at Kelvington.
Permit me to recapitulate. During the recent election campaign Mr. Ferrie, who represented the Mackenzie constituency in the last narliament, was able to ask, "What did Nicholson bring back to this constituency? I have brought back two post offices, one at Kelvington and one at Carrot River".
I bear Mr. Ferrie no ill will whatsoever. Indeed, I am greatly indebted to him for having given me a chance to relax for a few years. When you have been here eight or nine years you really should have a change. However, I was at one of Mr. Ferrie's meetings at a time when he mentioned that he was able to bring a post office to Kelvington, and one to Carrot River. I think hon. members will agree that no hon. member, regardless of party, should seek support on the basis that he decides where post offices should be built.
When this report appeared in the Kelvington paper to the effect that there was to be an item of $110,000 in the estimates this year, I was somewhat disturbed. In his letter to me Mr. Fletcher stated:
The enclosed notice was in last week's Kelvington Radio. I was in to the editor's place yesterday renewing my paper and he showed me the letter he had received with this notice. It was on House of Commons stationery and signed by G. M. Ferrie and had no postage. Besides the insult to you of sending the notification by the defeated member he is still using the franking privileges of a member . . .

When he brings in the 5-cent postage stamp I hope he will put plenty of glue on it so it will stick to the letters, because the arguments advanced in this house certainly are not convincing as to the justification for the increase which he proposes.
I would say that the evidence or rather the figures we have before us, and the reasons given by the Postmaster General for this needed increase, certainly do not conform to the principle he himself laid down. As reported at page 1102 of Hansard, at the conclusion of his remarks at the introduction of his resolution, he said:
I believe everyone will also agree that the most equitable arrangement is for the cost of service to be borne by the users, and this is exactly the object of the present resolution.

want to have to subsidize second-ciass mail such as periodicals and newspapers, and are very resentful over this action on the part of the government, which just prior to the election removed the excise stamp from cheques and now are imposing a new tax upon the Canadian people.
I particularly want to register my protest against this increase in postage rates for the simple reason that many of us are quite resentful of the fact that we are paying for or are subsidizing second-class mail such as periodicals, which carry a great deal of advertising matter and certainly no essential information to our people. I agree that in this country our newspapers and periodicals perform a very useful service in distributing knowledge and information to our people; but I went down to the reading room here and looked through some of the periodicals which enjoy the privilege of being subsidized by our Canadian taxpayers. In one magazine I found that there were no less than 32 full pages of liquor advertisements. That magazine enjoys a subsidy from the Canadian taxpayers.
I do not believe that situation is fair or just to our Canadian taxpayers. Furthermore, I should like to bring to the minister's attention the fact that when we find some places, particularly in our rural areas, where services are being cut, it does not seem opportune for the minister to introduce this increase in postage rates.
I should like to bring to his attention a matter in my own constituency, where we have just recently had a curtailment of mail service. 1 refer specifically to the case of the C.P.R. Reston-Wolseley line, where we formerly had the services of a mail clerk. Recently I had a letter from a constituent who, incidentally, was one of the key Liberal supporters and organizers in that constituency. Therefore I want to join with those who support the action of the leader of the C.C.F. party in moving the six months' hoist, which will have the effect that the bill will not come up again this session. I think it is even in the interests of the government and in the interests of justice and fairness to all concerned that the government should reconsider this measure before trying to force it through the house.

Mr. Speaker, before the vote is taken I should like to say a few words. At the resolution stage I did not make any contribution to the debate other than to ask a question of the Postmaster General. I asked him to explain an apparent inconsistency in the entire government argument for an increase in postal rates. In the minister's statement the other day he completely ignored what I believe to be the fundamental question involved in the entire bill which seeks to increase postal rates. At page 1764 of Hansard for yesterday the minister said:
As I said in the debate on the resolution, if we adopt the principle that postal revenue need not meet expenditures but that the revenues of the department should be supplemented by tax money, then we should have a truly subsidized service.
The implication there is that at the present time we do not have a subsidized service. The implication is that at the present time the post office is paying its way, but that the establishment of a subsidized system is going to come about if we do not increase the postal rates. Many hon. members have pointed out to the minister that at the present time when a man places a 4-cent stamp on a letter, that stamp not only pays for all the services which the sender of the letter receives but does more. Up until this year-perhaps it might also happen next year; we do not know-it has taken care of the deficit on second-class mail service, and it provided the post office with a surplus of over $6 million last year.
If the minister is logical in his assertion that the post office must pay its own way, then I say that the person who places a 4cent stamp on a letter today is paying for the service he receives. As a matter of fact a 3-cent stamp today would be a fair charge to the sender for the carrying of his letter. Now the government proposes to increase the rate to five cents, and as yet the minister has failed to explain this inconsistency. If the Post Office Department is going to be required to pay its operating expenses out of its revenues, then I want to ask the minister to explain to the house how he can justify the continuance of the subsidy on second-class mail.
The minister has not mentioned a word about the subsidy. It is accepted; it is not even questioned by the government. It is going to continue, and the senders of first-class mail who now pay three or four cents on their letters are going to be required to pay four or five cents. In other words they are now going to be asked to bear an additional burden in order to maintain a subsidy on second-class mail.

It seems to me that this is the crux of the whole matter, notwithstanding all the reasons that have been advanced for the increase in postal rates. Certain members to my right have suggested that there is a subsidy to Trans-Canada Air Lines. I was interested in reading an editorial in the Toronto Star of February 2 headed "Air Mail Cheapest by T.C.A." The editorial points out that the T.C.A. tariff for carrying air mail is $1.39 per ton mile, that the tariff charged by the private air lines, the largest of which is Canadian Pacific, averages $3.06 per ton mile, and that the lowest tariff charged by a private air line in this country is $2.79 per ton mile. In other words, T.C.A. is carrying mail at less than half the cost that is being paid by the Post Office Department for the transportation of mail by private carriers.
I have heard at least two or three members make reference to a subsidy to Trans-Canada Air Lines, but I notice they are never much concerned about subsidies to private air lines. All the reasons that have been advanced skirt the main issue, which must of course be the question of what is going to be done about second-class mail. In the statement made by the minister when he introduced the bill and in the statement he made yesterday he completely ignored the question of second-class mail. Before we are called upon to vote on this matter we should have a statement from the minister explaining how he can justify the position the government is taking, that the Post Office Department must meet its current expenses out of revenues, in view of the continued existence of the subsidy on second-class mail.
There is one other point I should like to mention. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is in his seat. When the minister was giving estimates of the increased cost next year he estimated the cost of introducing the five-day 40-hour week at $5 million. There must be some basis upon which that estimate was made. Surely the Post Office Department must have had some idea of how many and what post offices would be involved. Apparently the Minister of Finance was able to assure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) this afternoon that Winnipeg was one of the cities.

Mr. Speaker, at this time of evening I shall attempt to answer some of the arguments which have been made, and I shall endeavour not to indulge in any repetition. I shall deal first with some of the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), since they cover most of the objections raised on the other side of the house.
With some heat, the Leader of the Opposition seemed to object to what he repeatedly termed a political speech on my part. What I had done was quote from the Woods-Gordon report, give a clear-cut statement of the financial position of the department and make, I think, some proper observations in regard to the tactics of the opposition. He, and he alone, however, seemed to resent my doing so.
I repeat that there was no thought in my mind of making a political speech, in the ordinary sense of the term; but his reply was, I submit, political from beginning to end. After trying to create an atmosphere of confusion he then proceeded to flog a dead horse in discussing the tabling of the Woods-Gordon report. When I listened to his remarks, made in a loud and scolding tone, I thought I must have been guilty of something improper-only to find that, in fact, what he was doing was commending me for my action in tabling the report.
I am suggesting to him that the next time he agrees with me, he should not do it so violently. May I ask him also not to keep on repeating, and by his repetition encourage the idea, that there is nothing illegal about posting letters in the United States in order

to evade paying the proper rate of postage in this country. As I informed the house earlier Canada, along with some 90 other countries, is signatory to the universal postal union conventions and documents; and under the terms of these international agreements and by regulations having the full force of law, it is absolutely illegal for anyone to attempt to evade postal rates in one country by depositing his mail in another. The penalties which I have mentioned would undoubtedly apply.
Moreover, United States postal authorities would not countenance such a practice. If the Leader of the Opposition, instead of reading "Alice in Wonderland" and quoting from it, would turn to section 5 (1) (j) of the Post Office Act he would see how wrong he is in what he had to say on this question of depositing mail in another country. I shall help my hon. friend in that respect by quoting this paragraph. It says that the Postmaster General may-
(j) make and give effect to any postal agreement or arrangement with the government or postal authorities of any country or independent postal administration and pay out of postal revenue any remuneration or indemnity thereby provided.
That is exactly what we did. As I said before, Canada is bound by that treaty under the universal postal union. What I said before really applies. The Post Office Act does, I admit, make dull reading; but if, again, my hon. friend wishes to be authoritative he will have to give up his light reading, at least for a time.
His reference once more to Sir William Mulock, a tribute which good Liberals always enjoy, overlooked one fundamental point-that increased volume would net profits only if the per item rate is in itself profitable. It reminds me of the merchant who was going bankrupt and could not understand why. He knew he was losing money on each item he sold, but he was always hoping that the volume of business he was doing would permit him to make a profit.
Another, and not the last, item on which the Leader of the Opposition attempted to misinterpret what I said was when he said I had claimed that the opposition supported the idea that $13,500,000 added revenue could be obtained only in the way I suggested. Never at any time did I say anything of the kind. Once more may I suggest that the Leader of the Opposition give up reading "Alice in Wonderland" and pay more attention to what is said in the house.

I then went on to spell out in detail the items making up this cost and to summarize what the opposition had suggested as an alternative to the straightforward method of increasing postage rates.
The Leader of the Opposition tried to make some point of the fact that the government paid its telephone bills and other charges for similar services. I am sure no one would suggest that the government could do anything else, particularly when telephone service is provided by private concerns. But in the case of the Post Office Department, for other departments to pay their postage would simply be taking money out of one pocket and putting it in another, a bookkeeping device which would not change the over-all picture in any particular.
I cannot understand my hon. friend's excitement about a reference to using taxes to meet increased postal charges. He denied emphatically ever having suggested anything of the kind. Once more, I did not say that he himself had made the suggestion. I said that this had come from the opposition. It was, therefore, exceedingly amusing to find his stalwart supporter, the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken), repeating most emphatically this same suggestion a little later on. I think this is a complete answer to my hon. friend.
Then if I follow correctly the order of his remarks he came again to the idea that while

we lost some $7,500,000 in the stamp tax we did have substantial savings in the cost of handling these items. I had already informed him that the costs were in the neighbourhood of $30,000, so the balance sheet of this particular item would be: lost revenue, $7,500,000; gain in lowered cost of handling, $30,000; net loss, $7,470,000. In other words we would be losing 99-6 per cent and managing to hold the other -4 per cent.
There was one thing I was glad to note, however, in the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition. He disagreed with the junior addition to his ranks, the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace (Mr. Hamilton), who had earlier sneered at and derided the tribute paid by the Woods-Gordon company to departmental officials. I thank the Leader of the Opposition for his tribute to these same men, and commend his attitude to his back-row supporter.
I come now to the question of abolishing the post office savings bank and the repeated suggestion that there would be a clear saving of $377,000. There would indeed be a saving of this amount to the Post Office Department, but may I submit that it does not follow there would be a saving of that amount or perhaps of any amount to the government at large.
The savings bank is widely used and I am sure is an appreciated service. Some $37 million stays on deposit over many years and this money is made available to the government, thus lowering the amount it may need to raise by way of loan. The difference between the $377,000 cost of operation and the cost of short-term bank loans, with any administration costs, would be the only saving possible by the abolition of the bank.
While I am on the subject of the bank, which was also mentioned by many others, it is interesting to know that if the government does decide to implement this particular recommendation we will be able to assure depositors who might be somewhat disappointed by our action that the opposition were all enthusiastic for this course of action.
With regard to the reference to the $200,000, and some other items mentioned in the Woods-Gordon report, which could be saved in Toronto alone, again we have in the observations of the opposition the idea that Toronto is just one relatively small district, and that we can multiply manyfold the suggested savings to such a degree that $13,500,000 will be realized in a very short time. In actual fact approximately one-fifth of postal costs are incurred in Toronto, since about one-fifth of the whole mail handled passes through that area.

If we accepted, then, the estimated savings nf the Woods-Gordon report and apply these same savings everywhere, we could not hope to realize any more than a small fraction of the $13,500,000. To make this small fraction a little more proportionate than that term would indicate, may I suggest that a maximum saving of $2 million might be possible, not an insignificant amount by any means but still a long way short of the $15 million we will realize and need under the proposal now before the house.
Now I come to one phase of the remarks of my hon. friend opposite which pained me greatly, that is, the outspoken commendation he gave to the methods employed by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace in gathering information about the Woods-Gordon report. He counsels and encourages hon. members to follow such a course, but I am sure others were shocked by the action and perhaps even more shocked by the attitude of the Leader of the Opposition with respect to it. Then there are two bills in the name of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham), one with respect to the boundary between the provinces of Ontario and Manitoba and one with respect to the Explosives Act. Then there is second reading of the amendment to the Canadian Forces Act. We shall take them in that order on Monday and Tuesday.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
